title: Not Plato's Republic
hook: don't hope for a perfect world; be content if the smallest thing goes forward (Meditations 9.29)

segments.voice: Yesterday: correct, or be kind. Your line was who's stopping you. Which did you choose, and was it what the moment needed? Day six hundred eleven.

The town meeting runs all evening and ends with a vote to study the issue further. The group project has one person doing all the work. The world's problems are so big you can't even find the edge of one to hold on to. It's easy to decide that nothing you do matters unless it fixes everything. Marcus ran an empire, and in book nine he answered that pull with a five-word line. Today: rushing river.
screen: `ALL EVENING, NO DECISION.` → `IT MATTERS ONLY IF IT FIXES ALL?` → `NOT PLATO'S REPUBLIC.`

segments.voice: First, the torrent. Marcus begins: the cause of all things is like a rushing river; it carries everything along. And how cheap, he says, are the little men who play at statesmanship and imagine they're doing philosophy. Second, the line. Then, in George Long's 1862 translation: “Do not expect Plato's Republic.” Plato wrote a whole dialogue imagining the perfect city, ruled by philosophers. Marcus, a ruler who wrote philosophy, tells himself not to expect it. Instead, be content if the smallest thing goes forward, and don't think that outcome is a small matter. Third, why. Who, he asks, can change people's beliefs? And without a change of belief, what do you get but people groaning while they pretend to obey? Force can make a law. It can't make a heart agree. Fourth, the plain work. Marcus mentions famous rulers, Alexander and Philip among them, and says if they only played the tragic hero, no one has sentenced him to copy them. The work of philosophy, he writes, is simple and modest; don't lead me into pomposity. He also tells himself to do what nature asks right now, without looking around to see whether anyone will know. So the hope isn't the perfect city. It's the next small thing, moved forward one honest inch.
screen: `EVERYTHING IN A RUSHING RIVER.` · `DON'T EXPECT THE PERFECT CITY.` · `FORCE CAN'T CHANGE BELIEFS.` · `SIMPLE AND MODEST WORK.` · then, large: `THE SMALLEST THING.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Pick one problem that feels too big: in your work, your family, your town, the world. Hold it for a breath, and let it be too big. Now look for the smallest thing in it that could go forward this week. One email. One conversation. One bag of litter. One hour of help. Make it small enough that you could actually do it. See yourself doing it. The bell holds the time.
Rushing river. Marcus's image for the cause of all things, carrying everything along; even so, he asks only that the smallest thing move forward. Today's word.
Your line: the smallest thing. Move one small thing forward today, and don't call it small. Day six hundred eleven.

howItsDone: People who take this line seriously tend to set small, concrete goals inside big problems, and count each small step as real progress rather than waiting for a complete solution.

fork.reveal: do not expect Plato's Republic, he writes. force can't change beliefs, so he aims for small, real progress, and calls it no small matter.

original.note: Greek: the Republic, Plato's dialogue about the ideal city; the word means a constitution, a city's way of life.

trapdoor: what you thought: lower your expectations.
what it means: don't wait for a perfect world before acting; move the smallest thing forward, and count it.
what a scholar hears: in the Republic, Plato imagines a city ruled by philosophers; here a ruler who wrote philosophy tells himself not to expect that city.

notes: Confirm Long's wording in 9.29: 'Do not expect Plato's Republic: but be content if the smallest thing goes on well, and consider such an event to be no small matter.' Only the first clause is quoted.

9.29 paraphrased: the universal cause as a torrent; 'poor political men' who think they play the philosopher; do what nature requires now and don't look about to see if anyone will know; who can change men's opinions; Alexander, Philip, Demetrius of Phalerum; 'simple and modest is the work of philosophy; draw me not aside to insolence and pride.' Confirm.
'Five-word line' in the hook counts 'Do not expect Plato's Republic' (five words). 'Often called the nearest thing to a philosopher-king' is a common description, hedged.
